passage: When the Indian librarian S. R. Ranganathan introduced his colon classification in 1933, most library systems gave each book a single fixed number drawn from a predetermined list of subjects, so a work that touched on two fields had to be filed under just one of them. Ranganathan proposed a different principle. Rather than slot each work into one prearranged category, his system built a call number out of separate facets, such as subject, place, and time, that could be combined as a particular book required. The arrangement let a catalog represent works that fit no single heading, which the older fixed schemes could not easily do.
question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.text: Ranganathan worked as a librarian in India for years before he published his classification system in 1933.
Ranganathan's system built each call number from combinable facets, letting it represent works that fixed single-category schemes could not easily place.
Before 1933, most library systems gave every book a single fixed number drawn from a predetermined list of subjects.
Ranganathan's system proved hard to adopt because it required librarians to master an unfamiliar set of facets.

explanation: The correct answer is B. The passage contrasts the older fixed-category systems with Ranganathan's faceted approach and stresses what the new approach made possible: representing books that fit no single heading. Choice B captures that central contribution. Choice A reports only a biographical detail, and choice C states only the background problem the system was meant to solve. Choice D raises a difficulty of adoption that the passage never mentions, so it cannot be the main idea.
